title: Supreme Court Says No to New Missouri Voting Map
summary:
Imagine you and your friends are picking teams for a game. Now imagine one team gets to draw the lines that decide who plays where. That's what's happening in Missouri right now — but with voting maps.

On Thursday, the U.S. Supreme Court said no to a new map that Republicans in Missouri wanted to use. The court said the old map — made in 2022 — must be used for the elections this November. Those elections will help decide who controls the House of Representatives in Washington, D.C.

The new map was designed to help Republicans win seven of Missouri's eight House seats. Right now, they hold six. The map would have split up a Kansas City area represented by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver.

This fight has been going on for more than a year. People who didn't like the new map collected hundreds of thousands of signatures to try to force a statewide vote on it. They turned in the signatures in December. But Missouri's Secretary of State, Denny Hoskins, waited until August to say no to the petition.

Then Missouri's top court said Hoskins had to put the question on the November ballot — and that the new map was never really a law. Hoskins didn't follow that order, so a judge said he had to come to court on Thursday to explain why. The U.S. Supreme Court's decision means the old map stays for now.
why_it_matters: Voting maps decide whose votes carry the most power, so learning how the lines get drawn helps you understand why every election rule matters.

questions.question: What did the U.S. Supreme Court say about the voting map on Thursday?
options: It said the old map from 2022 must be used
It said the new map could be used
It said Missouri needed a brand-new map
It said the map question was up to the President
questions.correct_answer: It said the old map from 2022 must be used

Win seats in the U.S. Senate
Win seven of Missouri's eight House seats
Lose control of the House of Representatives

background_read: Missouri (a state in the middle of the United States) is one of many states that redraw their voting maps, and the U.S. Supreme Court (the country's highest court) is often asked to settle fights about those maps.
Every 10 years the United States counts everyone who lives there, and states use those numbers to redraw their voting maps — so the lines can change after each count.
The House of Representatives (the part of Congress that makes laws for the whole country) has 435 seats, and each state gets a share based on how many people live there.
Article_Structure: WHO: The U.S. Supreme Court, Missouri Republicans, Missouri's Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, and voters who signed a petition.
WHAT: The Supreme Court said no to a new voting map, so the old map made in 2022 will be used for the November elections.
WHERE: Missouri, including a Kansas City area represented by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver.
WHY: The map could change who wins Missouri's House seats, and those seats help decide who controls the House of Representatives in Washington, D.C.

perspectives.description: They say the map made in 2022 was already approved, so the Supreme Court was right to keep it for the November elections.
They believe new lines would be fairer or would help their party win more seats, and they are upset the change was blocked.
They wanted the people of Missouri to vote on the map themselves, and they are glad the question went to court and toward the ballot.
